displayQuote: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds

meta.title: Who really said "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Oppenheimer — but he did not say it at the Trinity test. He said it in a filmed NBC interview twenty years later, describing a line he remembered thinking: Bhagavad Gita 11.32, in his own translation, learned in Sanskrit from Arthur Ryder at Berkeley.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds'?
meta.ogDescription: His words, and his own translation of Gita 11.32 — but spoken to a television camera in 1965, not at the bomb test in 1945. His brother remembers him saying 'It worked.'

answer.label: Verified — but in a 1965 interview, not at Trinity
answer.authorDates: 1904–1967 · theoretical physicist, director of Los Alamos
answer.sourceLine: The words are his, and the scene is wrong. Oppenheimer spoke them on camera for the NBC White Paper documentary The Decision to Drop the Bomb (1965), produced by Fred Freed, describing what he remembered in the seconds after the Trinity test of 16 July 1945: ‘I remembered the line from the Hindu scripture, the Bhagavad-Gita…’ He is quoting Bhagavad Gita 11.32, in his own English rendering — he had read the poem in Sanskrit under Arthur Ryder at Berkeley. What he actually said aloud in the desert, according to his brother Frank, was closer to ‘I guess it worked.’

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Decision to Drop the Bomb, NBC White Paper
Bhagavad Gita 11.32, in Oppenheimer’s own translation
Trinity test, 16 July 1945 — recalled twenty years later

source.excerpt: We waited until the blast had passed, walked out of the shelter and then it was extremely solemn. We knew the world would not be the same. A few people laughed, a few people cried. Most people were silent. I remembered the line from the Hindu scripture, the Bhagavad-Gita: Vishnu is trying to persuade the Prince that he should do his duty and, to impress him, he takes on his multi-armed form and says, "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." I suppose we all thought that, one way or another.
trail: The primary source is film, which is unusually good provenance: Oppenheimer says the words to camera, in his own voice, and the footage survives. The framing is explicit and he does not overclaim — ‘I remembered the line’, and then ‘I suppose we all thought that’ the passage ↗.

Witnesses at Trinity remember something else entirely. His brother Frank Oppenheimer, who was there, recalled that what got said was along the lines of ‘It worked.’ General Farrell’s contemporaneous account describes relief and exhaustion rather than scripture the witness accounts ↗.

Two honest limits. First, we cannot rule out that the Gita line crossed his mind at the moment — he says it did, and nobody can check a thought. Second, sources disagree about the earliest printed appearance: the November 1948 Time profile of Oppenheimer is cited by some scholars, while others put the earliest citation they could verify at 1964. We have not inspected the 1948 page ourselves, so we flag the disagreement rather than pick a winner Hijiya, ‘The Gita of J. Robert Oppenheimer’ ↗.
source.excerptNote: The full passage as broadcast. Two things stand out once you read it whole. He never claims to have spoken the line — he says he remembered it, and then hedges even that with ‘I suppose’. And he says Vishnu, where the Gita has Krishna speaking; Krishna is an avatar of Vishnu, so it is a compression rather than an error, but it is his compression, not the text’s.
source.rightsNote: Oppenheimer’s words are in copyright. He died in 1967, so his spoken text is protected in the UK and EU until the end of 2037, and the 1965 NBC broadcast is separately protected as an audiovisual work with its own rights holder — quoting the sentence is one thing, reusing the footage is another. The Sanskrit of the Bhagavad Gita is ancient and free; this English wording is not the Gita, it is Oppenheimer’s translation of it, and translations carry their own copyright. Arthur Ryder’s competing rendering has its own status again. Attribute, quote briefly, and do not treat the footage as stock. This is not legal advice.

author.name: J. Robert Oppenheimer
author.heading: About J. Robert Oppenheimer
author.metaLine: 1904–1967 · theoretical physicist, director of Los Alamos
author.bio: J. Robert Oppenheimer (1904–1967) directed the Los Alamos laboratory that designed the first nuclear weapons, and spent the rest of his life arguing for international control of them — a campaign that ended with his security clearance revoked in 1954. The Sanskrit was not an affectation: he learned the language at Berkeley under the Indologist Arthur Ryder in the 1930s, read the Bhagavad Gita in the original, kept a copy on his desk and gave copies to friends. When he reached for it in 1965, he was reaching for something he had actually read.

misattribution.heading: The scene is the problem, not the speaker
misattribution.intro: The man is right and the words are right. What everyone gets wrong is when and how — and once you fix the scene, the line reads quite differently.

items.why: The standard picture — Oppenheimer at the test site, intoning it as the fireball rises — has no support. He said the words to a television camera in 1965 and described them as something he remembered. His brother Frank, who was standing there, recalled the actual words being closer to ‘It worked’ the witness accounts ↗.

items.who: His own, not a standard one
items.why: Gita 11.32 opens with the Sanskrit kālo ’smi. Most translators render that word as time — a devouring, world-ending time. Oppenheimer chose Death, and the archaic ‘am become’ gives it a King James cadence the Sanskrit does not have. His own Sanskrit teacher, Arthur Ryder, had translated the passage as ‘Death am I, and my present task. / Destruction.’ The famous version is Oppenheimer’s literary decision on the verse ↗.

items.scope: Who is speaking in the Gita
items.why: In the 1965 interview he says Vishnu. In the poem it is Krishna, revealing his cosmic form to the reluctant prince Arjuna. Krishna is an avatar of Vishnu, so this is compression rather than error — but if you are quoting the Gita, quote Krishna.

items.scope: The ‘brighter than a thousand suns’ line
items.who: A different verse, often merged in
items.why: The thousand-suns image comes from a neighbouring passage of the same chapter and is frequently spliced into accounts of Trinity alongside this one. Later biographical writing runs them together; Oppenheimer’s own 1965 account uses only the death passage.

items.who: Whether he thought it at the time
items.why: He says he remembered the line as the blast passed. Nobody can verify a thought twenty years after the fact, and some contemporaries were sceptical that the memory took its final shape that day. We record the doubt without resolving it.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Oppenheimer — his own translation of Bhagavad Gita 11.32, spoken on camera for NBC in 1965 as a memory of the Trinity test, not as a line delivered at it the passage ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The grammar is the whole thing. Not ‘I have become’ but ‘I am become’ — an archaic construction that describes a state arrived at rather than an act performed. It gives the sentence the flatness of something being reported rather than confessed, which is why it survives repetition so well.

It also fits the source better than most people realise. In the Gita, Krishna is telling a soldier who wants to refuse battle that the destruction is already underway and his part in it is his duty. That is a great deal closer to the position Oppenheimer was in than the line’s usual use as a cry of guilt.
context.detailsSummary: Trinity, and what was actually said
detailsBody: 16 July 1945, 5:29am, Alamogordo Bombing Range, New Mexico: the first detonation of a nuclear device, a plutonium implosion design, yield around 21 kilotons.
Frank Oppenheimer, present at the test, recalled the words spoken as being along the lines of ‘I guess it worked.’
Kenneth Bainbridge, the test director, is reported to have said something considerably blunter to Oppenheimer afterwards.
The Gita passage appears in Oppenheimer’s own telling twenty years later, on film, framed as a memory.

Sources disagree on the earliest printed appearance of the line in connection with him — a November 1948 Time profile is cited by some scholars, 1964 by others. We flag the disagreement rather than assert a date.
context.pull: He said it to a camera in 1965. What his brother remembers from the desert is 'It worked.'
